title: Salsa Verde
subtitle: Roasted green pepper and jalapeño salsa with coriander and lime
excerpt: A roasted green salsa made from charred green peppers, jalapeños, onion, garlic, and coriander. A UK adaptation using green peppers in place of tomatillos, which aren't widely available. Bright, tangy, and works as a table salsa or cooking sauce for enchiladas.
sourceNotes: Salsa verde: traditionally made with tomatillos (Physalis philadelphica), which are not widely available in the UK. This version uses roasted green peppers and jalapeños to achieve a similar flavour profile: sharp, green, and slightly smoky. The method follows the standard charred tomatillo approach adapted for the available ingredients. Synthesised from Mexican cooking sources with UK ingredient substitutions.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in small portions for up to 3 months. Defrost in the fridge overnight.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a larger batch and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Improves overnight in the fridge. Use as a table salsa or as the sauce for enchiladas suizas.

content.text: Salsa verde is traditionally made with tomatillos, small green husk tomatoes with a sharp, fruity flavour. They are not widely available in the UK. This version uses roasted green peppers and jalapeños instead, which achieves a similar profile: a sharp, green, slightly smoky salsa that works as a table condiment or a cooking sauce. The cooking method is the same: char under a high grill, then blend.

items.prepNote: halved; keep seeds for more heat, remove for mild

content.text: Note: this is a UK adaptation using green peppers instead of tomatillos. The flavour is similar, sharp and green, but somewhat milder and sweeter. A squeeze of extra lime juice at the end compensates for the lower acidity of peppers compared to tomatillos.

Heat the grill to its highest setting. Lay the green pepper halves (skin side up), jalapeños, onion quarters, and unpeeled garlic on a baking tray. Drizzle with {{olive-oil}} of olive oil and season with salt.
Grill for 15-20 minutes until the peppers have blackened patches and the flesh is completely soft. The garlic should feel soft when pressed.

Leave to cool for 5 minutes. Peel and discard the garlic skins and the blackened pepper skins if they come off easily (don't worry about getting all the skin). Transfer everything, including the cooking juices, to a blender with the coriander and lime juice.
Blend to a rough, textured consistency. Taste and adjust with more lime juice and salt. The salsa should taste bright and sharp.

items.symptom: Salsa tastes sweet rather than sharp
items.cause: Green peppers are sweeter than tomatillos; too little lime
items.fix: Add more lime juice. This is the most important correction. The sharpness is what makes the salsa taste fresh rather than just cooked green vegetable.

items.cause: Peppers not very juicy, or cooked juices discarded
items.fix: Make sure all the cooking juices go into the blender. Thin with a splash of cold water if needed after blending.

items.symptom: Not hot enough for the table
items.fix: Leave some seeds in next time, or add a pinch of chilli powder to the blender.

items.symptom: Skin still visible in the salsa as chewy pieces
items.cause: Pepper skins not peeled after grilling
items.fix: Pull off as many of the blackened pepper skins as come away easily after cooling. Small remaining pieces blend in fine; large pieces are chewy.

content.text: Salsa verde using tomatillos is one of the fundamental Mexican cooking sauces, used on tacos, tamales, enchiladas, and as a table condiment across the country. Tomatillos are sold in some specialist shops and a few UK supermarkets. If you find them, use 500g of tomatillos in place of the green peppers in this recipe; halve them and grill the same way. The result will be sharper and more complex than the pepper version.
